summary: Sets out routing requirements for home control and automation applications on low-power and lossy networks. It covers devices like sensors, actuators and controllers that have short radio range and rely on routing. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Home automation networks connect switches, sensors, controllers, and actuators, many of which have limited radio range and power. RFC 5826 lists routing requirements for these networks, including response time, automatic setup, and routes that account for device constraints.

questions: what is a low power and lossy network
how many devices must a home automation routing protocol support
subtitle: Routing requirements for wireless home-control devices with limited range, power, and memory.

tldr.problem: Home automation devices often have short radio range, limited resources, and links that can become unreliable as conditions change.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes home-control use cases and gives routing requirements for constrained paths, mobility, convergence, manageability, and stability.
tldr.outcome: The Informational document sets targets including support for at least 250 devices and convergence within 0.5 seconds when nodes have not moved.

facts.label: Convergence when nodes have not moved

today: RFC 5826 is Informational and was published in April 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Home Automation over Lossy Links
sections.content:
Home automation networks may include wall switches, water-leak sensors, heating valves, controllers, and other devices. A node can be both a sensor and an actuator. Because radio range is limited, traffic may need to pass through other devices.

Nodes can have limited battery, memory, and CPU resources. People moving, doors opening, or appliances starting can change radio reception. The RFC says all traffic in a ROLL network is carried as IPv6 packets and that its requirements can also apply to other low-power links.
sections.plainLanguage: Home devices may need other nodes to forward their messages. Their links can change, and many devices have limited power and memory.

sections.title: Home-Control Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC describes coordinated lighting, energy management, moving remote controls, adding modules, window shades, video surveillance, healthcare, and alarms. One lighting event may activate many devices. A remote control should appear to respond within a few hundred milliseconds, while a new module should be included within a few seconds.

Battery-operated shades may sleep for much of the time, delaying a command until they wake. For alarms, routing through sleeping battery devices can delay delivery. The RFC advises using battery-powered safety devices for routing only when there is no other alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: Home applications range from lighting commands to alarms and health reports. Their routing needs differ, especially when devices sleep or users expect an immediate response.

sections.title: Routing and Convergence Requirements
sections.content:
The routing protocol must support at least 250 devices and should be extensible beyond that. It must support routes that account for node properties such as CPU, memory, energy level, sleep periods, and the difficulty of replacing a battery. It should prefer mains-powered nodes when possible.

The protocol must converge within 0.5 seconds when no nodes have moved and within four seconds when nodes have moved. These targets apply to a network of up to 250 nodes with up to four repeating nodes between source and destination. A new node must be able to obtain an address and join with almost no human intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing should account for power and device limits, support at least 250 nodes, and recover quickly after changes. New devices should be able to join without advanced manual configuration.

sections.title: Traffic and Network Stability
sections.content:
Traffic patterns depend on whether devices communicate directly or through a central controller. Wall switches may send only one to ten times per hour; sensors may report when queried or at intervals. Frames typically carry less than five bytes of payload, and interference can cause retransmissions.

A node that fails often should not be the first choice for forwarding traffic. Routing also needs to handle devices that move and links that become temporarily unreliable, while avoiding unnecessary battery use.
sections.plainLanguage: Many home devices send brief messages only occasionally. The routing protocol should avoid unreliable or frequently failing nodes when it can.

sections.title: Security and Joining Devices
sections.content:
The RFC requires the network to authenticate a new node before allowing it to affect routing decisions, and the routing protocol must support message integrity. It should defend against denial-of-service attacks and limit the effect of a compromised device.

The document recognizes a convenience tradeoff during device inclusion and says the network key may be exposed for short periods during that process. Electronic door locks and other critical applications should add end-to-end application security.
sections.plainLanguage: A device must authenticate before it can influence routing. Critical applications should add their own end-to-end protection.
